analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9950 probability of malware, and all 20 top n-grams contribute positively toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.007 to +0.016). The evidence falls into two groups that fit hashing or mining compute kernels. (1) SIMD-heavy data shuffling and mixing: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.016187), PXOR PXOR (+0.014516), MOVDQA PXOR (+0.008417), PXOR MOVDQA (+0.008342), MOVDQA PAND (+0.010762), MOVDQU PAND (+0.009485), MOVDQU MOVDQA (+0.007531), MOVDQA MOVAPS (+0.007602), LEA PXOR (+0.007141), MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.009895), MOVHLPS MOVQ (+0.007917), MOVQ MOVQ (+0.007259) and ADD MOVQ (+0.009029). PXOR and PAND combined with 128-bit moves and lane packing or unpacking are typical of vectorized state mixing in memory-hard or ARX-style hash functions. (2) Scalar rotate/shift/carry arithmetic: ADD ROR (+0.010480), XOR ROL (+0.008494), MOV ROL (+0.008028), ROL ADD (+0.007144), SHL OR (+0.007299), SUB ADC (+0.010338) and DIV MUL (+0.009561). Rotate-add-xor chains are the core of many hash round functions, and ADC/MUL/DIV suggest multi-precision arithmetic. PXOR PXOR (frequency 0.002097) and MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (0.003477) occur relatively often, which suggests the binary has sustained, repeated compute loops and not isolated incidental use. No single n-gram proves cryptojacking, and the evidence contains no function names, API calls or network indicators. The convergence of many independent crypto-style instruction patterns, together with the very high model probability, nonetheless strongly supports a cryptojacking classification.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top contributor. XOR-mixing of SIMD registers followed by an aligned 128-bit move is consistent with a vectorized hash round writing out its state. Its very low frequency suggests it is specific to a particular kernel.
Consecutive 128-bit XORs, at a relatively high frequency of 0.002097, indicate heavy vectorized XOR mixing, as in AES-like or Keccak/CryptoNight-style state updates.
Aligned load followed by a bitwise AND mask suggests SIMD bit masking or selection, as used in index extraction or lookup-table operations in hashing.
An add followed by a rotate is the ARX pattern found in many hash and cipher round functions.
Subtract followed by add-with-carry indicates multi-word big-integer arithmetic, which fits cryptographic or mining math.
Loading 64-bit values and packing them into a 128-bit register is a common step when preparing SIMD state. Its frequency of 0.003477 is the highest in the list, suggesting it recurs in hot loops.
Very rare (0.000002) but strongly weighted. Division and multiplication in sequence suggest wide-integer or modular arithmetic, as in memory-hard hash computation.
An unaligned SIMD load followed by masking indicates bulk data masking across buffers, consistent with scratchpad-style processing.
Scalar arithmetic feeding into SIMD/64-bit register transfers suggests mixed scalar and vector hash computation.
XOR combined with rotate-left is a classic hash and stream-cipher round primitive.
An aligned load followed by a SIMD XOR is consistent with XORing memory state into registers during a round.
The mirror of the previous pattern. XOR followed by a store or move completes a vectorized read-modify-write cycle in the mixing loops.
A scalar load followed by a rotate fits the register setup of rotate-based hash rounds.
Extracting the high half of an XMM register and moving it to a scalar is typical when combining or finalizing SIMD hash lanes.
Mixing integer and float-domain aligned moves is common in hand-optimized or compiler-vectorized state copies in crypto kernels.
Moving unaligned data into aligned working buffers suggests staged bulk data movement in a compute loop.
Shift-and-OR is the manual bit-rotation or field-packing idiom, consistent with hashing when it appears alongside ROL/ROR patterns.
Back-to-back 64-bit SIMD/scalar transfers suggest shuffling of 64-bit state words between registers.
A rotate followed by an add is another ARX-style round sequence, which reinforces the rotate-heavy hashing profile.
Address computation immediately before a SIMD XOR suggests indexed table or scratchpad lookups feeding XOR mixing, as in memory-hard algorithms.

key_indicators: Dense PXOR-based SIMD mixing (PXOR MOVAPS, PXOR PXOR, MOVDQA PXOR, PXOR MOVDQA, LEA PXOR)
SIMD masking and data movement (MOVDQA PAND, MOVDQU PAND, MOVDQU MOVDQA, MOVDQA MOVAPS)
Rotate/add/xor ARX patterns (ADD ROR, XOR ROL, MOV ROL, ROL ADD, SHL OR)
64-bit lane packing and extraction (MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ, MOVHLPS MOVQ, ADD MOVQ, MOVQ MOVQ)
All 20 top features push toward malware, with a model probability of 0.9950
analysis.recommended_action: Treat as a likely cryptominer. Confirm in a sandbox by looking for sustained high CPU use, mining-pool network connections (Stratum), and persistence mechanisms. Statically, locate the functions containing the PXOR/PAND and rotate-heavy loops and compare them against known hash implementations (e.g., CryptoNight, RandomX, Keccak, SHA-family). Extract any embedded wallet or pool configuration as IOCs, and isolate affected hosts if the binary was found in production.
